Writer, broadcaster, musician and kitchen gadget obsessive Carrie Marshall has been writing about tech since 1998, contributing sage advice and odd opinions to all kinds of magazines and websites as well as writing more than twenty books. Her latest, a love letter to music titled Small Town Joy, is on sale now. She is the singer in spectacularly obscure Glaswegian rock band Unquiet Mind.

articles.title: 4 ways to address the failures we found along the US border’s “virtual wall”
articles.text:
4 ways to address the failures we found along the US border’s “virtual wall”
The US has spent billions on surveillance towers, but hundreds of people have died near them. Here’s how to strengthen federal oversight.
MIT Technology Review today published our investigation into how many people have died near the “virtual wall” of surveillance towers that the US government has installed along the US-Mexico border.
We found cases of people who walked undetected through areas surveilled by advanced, AI-enabled towers and later died nearby, where their bodies remained unnoticed for weeks or months. These cases reflect systemic flaws in the virtual wall: broken towers, algorithms that failed to detect people, and agents who simply did not respond to alerts.
This story is part of Dying on Camera, a collaboration between MIT Technology Review and Times of San Diego. Journalists in both newsrooms spent the past year examining the failures of border surveillance technology and uncovering the stories of the people who die in the borderlands.
Each of these deaths should have raised alarms inside US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) about the flaws in the agency’s surveillance network. This is particularly true for cases near the latest towers built by the defense company Anduril, which continues to win major contracts and is poised to benefit from the windfall of federal money slated for border security. The US is set to spend $1 billion to triple the size of the virtual wall by 2034.
Here are four ideas for what CBP should do next to address these failures.
1. Conduct a comprehensive audit of deaths near the virtual wall
“If I were the federal government, I would do an audit, because this feels like it’s not working.”
That was New Mexico state representative Sarah Silva’s reaction when MIT Technology Review showed her that in 2024 alone, more than 18 people had died near surveillance towers in just one small stretch of desert near her district.
An audit is necessary because, despite poring over thousands of pages of police reports and other documents about surveillance towers, we have only limited knowledge of how many towers are out there and where they’re located.
CBP does not publish a comprehensive map of its virtual wall. We instead relied on mapping work led by the nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation and then used satellite imagery to verify where specific towers were and approximately when they were installed.
We analyzed lots of towers—nearly 600. But that’s still far less than the 800 the government says operate today. And our estimates of when they went up are inexact. That means our tally of more than 1,050 people who have died near them is an undercount. And we don’t have a complete picture of where along the border the problem is worst.
An internal audit would not have such limitations. In theory, CBP tracks when each tower went up and when it was active. It has had the ability to audit their effectiveness—while quantifying how many people have died near them—since at least 2015, when it began installing the types of towers included in our analysis. But sources told us it has never done such an audit. Our findings make the need for one more urgent.
2. Fix the way the agency tracks migrant deaths and remains
If CBP is to analyze instances where people have died near its surveillance technology, it needs to know when and where those deaths happen. And the current system for tracking that data is beyond broken.
As we note in our methodology, there is no national agency that collects and publishes all available records on migrant deaths. We sifted through thousands of pages of records from dozens of agencies in Texas alone, and our picture is still incomplete owing to the lack of a shared protocol for documenting these deaths in public records.
Border Patrol has had its own internal system, called the Border Safety Initiative Tracking System (BSITS), in place since 2007. But it wasn't until 2021 that national rules were established for how different sectors should enter cases into the system. The next year, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that many cases still weren't being tracked in this system, especially deaths that weren't discovered by Border Patrol. In 2023, the GAO reported that Border Patrol has taken steps to fix that, but outside researchers consistently find the agency’s estimates to be undercounts even today.
In addition to tracking migrant deaths, CBP launched a program in 2017 to prevent them, called the Missing Migrant Program. In April 2025, the GAO found the program was improving the way it collected and tracked data about events like 911 calls and rescues. The problem, it said, was that there was no plan in place to use the data to measure whether the program was actually increasing rescues or reducing deaths, which are its primary goals. It made two recommendations for solutions, neither of which has been implemented.
3. Track cases when surveillance technology leads to an apprehension
In 2014, when the virtual wall was much smaller, the GAO suggested that Border Patrol agents log when a piece of technology helped them apprehend someone who was trying to enter the US illegally. It would take agents some extra time, but logging these assists would help Congress understand how often various surveillance technologies were leading to actual apprehensions. Once this data was collected, GAO added, the agency should measure whether its surveillance technologies were working. CBP agreed, and it started requiring agents to enter such information.
Then, in 2017, the GAO reported that the data being collected was inaccurate and unreliable; it found agents in Texas, for example, who were crediting a specific type of tower in apprehensions hundreds of times, even though no such towers existed anywhere in the state. Border Patrol again said it would improve; it agreed to train agents on the importance of collecting such information.
But years later, agents told us, it’s still not a priority. One former CBP official described the mandate as “spitting in the wind, to be honest,” and said the messy reality of apprehensions doesn't translate into neat metrics. (The official, who requested anonymity, served during the Biden administration and wasn’t authorized to discuss sensitive issues.)
And in August 2021, more than seven years after it agreed to do so, CBP still had not produced any analysis on the towers’ effectiveness (it finished one in 2022, the GAO notes, but the results are not public).
That means the virtual wall is growing faster than anyone is assessing its impact.
4. Investigate deaths as potential surveillance failures
CBP should also examine new deaths as they occur and determine whether they happened within sight of a tower or other surveillance technology. And for those that did, the agency should determine why those people weren’t spotted sooner.
Several agents and officials told us that if Border Patrol agents come across the body of someone presumed to have died while crossing into the US, there’s no requirement to check whether that person died near surveillance infrastructure and no process for doing so. At a minimum, that means potentially valuable evidence about the death goes unexamined. It also means that migrant deaths are not routinely treated as possible failures of the virtual wall.
Do you have experience with border surveillance technology? We want to hear from you. Reach the reporters securely on Signal at jamesodonnell.22 and eileenguo.15 or tips@technologyreview.com.
CBP should automatically check every migrant death against its internal database of towers and investigate those that occurred within surveillance range to determine what the system detected and whether agents responded appropriately. Agents already log GPS coordinates when they apprehend a group or encounter footprints, among other events.
Without that check, law enforcement, medical investigators, and families may never learn that someone died near a surveillance tower—and that footage of the moments leading up to the death may exist. CBP typically deletes surveillance footage from the towers after 30 days unless an internal review is opened, which usually happens only for deaths in custody. At a minimum, flagging these cases could preserve footage for those investigating the death and give families a chance to request it.
Such reviews could also expose flaws in the virtual wall itself. Consider one location we identified in New Mexico, where several people died despite being in clear sight of an advanced AI tower. They died within the span of a few months, sometimes just hundreds of feet from one another. Investigating these cases might reveal, for example, that a camera repeatedly failed to detect or identify people in a particular area, or that agents were alerted and simply never responded.
Carrying out these postmortem inquiries would be the only way to answer the question that families, researchers, and volunteers raised most frequently in our investigation into the hundreds of migrants who died near towers: Did the cameras see them, and nobody came? Or did nobody see them at all?

articles.title: Studie zeigt: KI-Chatbots liefern bei Finanzfragen in 57 Prozent der Fälle falsche Antworten
articles.text:
Studie zeigt: KI-Chatbots liefern bei Finanzfragen in 57 Prozent der Fälle falsche Antworten
KI steht mittlerweile auch in Sachen Finanzberatung bei vielen Menschen hoch im Kurs. Doch sind die Finanztipps von KI-Chatbots auch gut? Laut einer Studie des Technologieunternehmens Saturn eher nicht. Populäre KI-Modelle wie ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Grok und Gemini lieferten demnach bei Finanzfragen im Durchschnitt in 57 Prozent der Fälle falsche Antworten.
Studie: KI-Chatbots machten Rechenfehler und halluzinierten
Bei komplexeren Fragen, die beispielsweise mehr als einen Rechenschritt erforderten, unterliefen den KI-Modellen im Durchschnitt sogar in 88 Prozent der Fälle Fehler. Einige Modelle lieferten gar bei 99 Prozent dieser schwierigeren Fragen falsche Antworten. Am besten schnitt das KI-Modell Claude Opus 5 im Reasoning-Modus ab, doch auch dieses machte bei 39 Prozent der Antworten Fehler.
Für die Studie wurden mehr als 100 verschiedene Fragen zu Finanzthemen an kostenlose und kostenpflichtige KI-Modelle von Anbietern wie ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude und Copilot gestellt. Den Studienergebnissen zufolge enthielten die KI-Antworten Rechenfehler, ließen anstehende Steueränderungen außer Acht oder halluzinierten und erfanden dabei Regeln, die es gar nicht gibt.
KI-Chatbot erfand Regel bei Studienkrediten, die es gar nicht gib
Im schlimmsten Fall kann das Vertrauen auf KI-Antworten bei Steuerfragen zu erheblichen finanziellen Verlusten führen. Amal Jolly, CEO von Saturn, erklärt gegenüber der Financial Times: „Millionen von Menschen vertrauen bei Finanzfragen auf KI-Modelle, erhalten jedoch falsche Antworten, die sie Geld kosten können.“ Wie die Untersuchung ergab, hätte ein Fehler bezüglich der Rentenbesteuerung durch das KI-Modell Claude Haiku 4.5 in Großbritannien dazu führen können, dass ein Sparer eine Nachzahlung von 17.500 Pfund (rund 20.400 Euro) an die britische Steuerbehörde HMRC hätte leisten müssen.
In einem anderen Fall „erfand“ Claude bei einer Frage zu Studienkrediten eine Regel und behauptete, Hochschulabsolvent:innen könnten die Rückzahlung einstellen, wenn sie ins Ausland ziehen. Das stimmt allerdings nicht.

articles.title: Amazon bloquea a Muse, la IA de Meta que puede comprar en línea por ti
articles.text:
Amazon le ha cerrado la puerta a Muse, el asistente de IA de Meta que puede controlar tu ordenador. A unos días de que se convirtiera en una de las aplicaciones más populares en móviles y debutara en la Mac, Muse no podrá realizar compras en Amazon usando tu cuenta de usuario. El gigante del comercio electrónico aseguró que el agente de Meta compraba en su tienda sin permiso ni aviso previo, por lo que decidió bloquearlo.
De acuerdo con GeekWire, Amazon bloqueó a Muse durante la noche del domingo. Cualquier usuario que intente usar al agente de Meta para comprar en la plataforma se encontrará con una notificación informando que no es posible. “El acceso continuo por parte de un agente de IA no autorizado viola las Condiciones de Uso de Amazon”, señala el mensaje.
Según Amazon, Meta nunca solicitó permiso para que su asistente operase dentro de la plataforma. La tecnológica añadió que Muse no se identifica cuando navega por el sitio y, según análisis internos, llega a capturar y almacenar las credenciales de los usuarios. Este punto es el que más ha preocupado a Amazon y sería el pretexto ideal para bloquear a la IA en su tienda en línea.
La IA de Meta no es la única que ha bloqueado Amazon
Aunque el bloqueo de Muse ha tomado relevancia por la relación que existe entre ambas empresas (Meta usa los chips Graviton para su IA), lo cierto es que no es el primer agente que sufre este veto. Amazon lleva varios meses cerrando la puerta a agentes externos de Google y OpenAI, así como a Perplexity, con quien tiene abierto un proceso judicial debido al navegador Comet.
Un portavoz de la compañía dijo que las aplicaciones que compran en tu nombre deben operar de forma transparente y respetar las decisiones de cada plataforma. Meta aseguró hace unos días que su agente no tiene visibilidad sobre las contraseñas ni métodos de pago de los usuarios, ya que usa un segundo sistema llamado Sentinel para procesar todas las operaciones.
Amazon añadió que su objetivo es proteger la experiencia de compra, pero también hay otra razón de peso: los anuncios. La plataforma tiene un negocio publicitario que registra ingresos de 68.000 millones de dólares al año. Esta cifra depende de que los usuarios naveguen por las páginas de su tienda y vean productos patrocinados, algo que no ocurre cuando le pides a un agente de IA que se encargue de comprar por ti.
Sumado a esto, Amazon tiene herramientas de compra asistida, como Alexa for Shopping y Buy for Me, que sí se identifican como una IA ante los comercios.
Muse no podrá acceder a una de las tiendas más grandes de internet
Meta aseguró hace unos días que su agente no tiene visibilidad sobre las contraseñas ni métodos de pago de los usuarios, ya que usa un segundo sistema para procesar todas las operaciones. A diferencia de Meta AI, Muse funciona como un agente capaz de ejecutar tareas completas en tu móvil o Mac. La IA se conecta con tu cliente de correo, calendario, notas y opera dentro de una máquina virtual segura con un navegador propio.
Para evitar que las cosas se salgan de control, los de Mark Zuckerberg implementaron un agente adicional conocido como Sentinel. Este aprueba cualquier acción que Muse envíe a internet y se encarga de procesar el sistema de pago y otros datos de forma segura, de modo que los servicios de Meta no puedan acceder a ellos. Muse se conecta con otros servicios y aplicaciones a través de APIs públicas, pero cuando el sistema no tiene una de estas, navega por la web como si fuera una persona.
Aunque esto es una mala noticia para los usuarios de Muse, la realidad es que no todos pueden comprar en línea usando la IA de Meta. Esta función solo está disponible en Estados Unidos a través de plataformas de terceros como Stripe o 1Password. De momento no existe una fecha definida para ofrecerla en otros países, como España, México, Argentina o el resto de América Latina.

articles.title: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
articles.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.
California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
Gavin Newsom signed a package of bills requiring AI data centers to pay for upgrades to the local energy grid.
Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements before qualifying for a streamlined approval process. Last week, Newsom signed an executive order to speed up the creation of an AI “kill switch.”
“While the Trump administration moves toward deregulation, communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom says in the press release. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.”

Its computer-vision software also sometimes isolated bumper stickers and other graphics, including, in one case, an American flag patch on a motorcyclist’s saddlebag.

articles.title: Corridor raises $25M seed to build a health benefits brokerage for SMBs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It’s been a while since Jackson Wagner left his job as a product lead at Scale AI in July 2022. Now, he’s building in a new space altogether: The new effort is an AI health benefits brokerage called Corridor that focuses on small businesses, which it says traditional brokerages often overlook because small accounts generate lower commissions even though they take the same amount of time as larger accounts.
Corridor is betting an AI solution may help on that front. On its platform, customers work with human advisors while AI agents do administrative tasks in the background. The company says its agents can handle tedious office work like checking whether a doctor is in a customer’s insurance network, scheduling care, or providing a doctor updated health insurance information.
“We are every single employee and management’s concierge for all things healthcare,” Nikhil Aggarwal, the company’s CEO, told TechCrunch.
On Monday, Corridor said it had raised a $25 million seed round led by Bain Capital Ventures.
Corridor came about after Wagner was in a running accident, and the poor handling of his care led him down a path of “significant, consistent, chronic pain.”
“I developed a long list of complications that needed to be worked through one by one,” he said.
He eventually left Scale AI to get a master’s degree in computer science and electrical engineering at UC Berkeley, before joining Build Robotics in 2023. Later, he teamed up with former Scale AI colleague Eric Qian to work on Capernaum AI, a startup building a clinical agent targeting musculoskeletal care and chronic pain.
The two eventually approached Cold Start to see if they would fund Capernaum, but Aggarwal, who was a partner at Cold Start along with Jason Dong, saw a much larger opportunity. So the four of them took off and launched Corridor together.
“Since health plans are the window through which the vast majority of Americans access healthcare, it became overwhelmingly clear that one of the highest impact things I could do to improve outcomes for individuals was to create a way for them to access better health plans,” Wagner said.
Other companies in this space include Ignition Benefits and Nava Benefits.
Investors in Corridor’s round include BoxGroup, as well as executives from OpenAI, Scale AI, and Ramp. The startup is now preparing for Q4, since “80% of small businesses choose their health plan in Q4,” Aggarwal said.
“Our vision is to build the most trusted healthcare institution in America,” he said. “To earn that, we are laser-focused on a simple promise: doing what we say we’re going to do for the businesses and employees we serve.”

articles.title: Why Nigeria’s FriendnPal is building an AI-powered mobile therapy service - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup FriendnPal is building an AI-powered behavioural health intelligence and remote patient monitoring platform designed to detect mental health risks earlier, close treatment gaps, intervene sooner, and deliver continuous care at scale.
Founded in 2023 by Esther Eruchie, following a deeply personal experience with mental health and the loss of her mother to depression, FriendnPal combines multimodal AI, behavioural analytics, digital phenotyping, clinical assessments, risk stratification, remote patient monitoring and human clinical triage to detect changes in behavioural and psychological patterns over time.
“Globally, mental healthcare is largely reactive, a person becomes symptomatic, seeks help, receives an assessment and is eventually connected to care, but FriendnPal is building the infrastructure to make care continuous, predictive and preventive,” Eruchie told Disrupt Africa.
FriendnPal does not position its AI as a replacement for clinicians, but rather a tool for them to use to better serve patients.
“Our AI identifies patterns and risk signals, where risk is detected, users can be triaged to licensed mental health professionals, creating a human-in-the-loop model of care. Our platform is designed for emerging markets, where affordability, language, geography and connectivity remain significant barriers,” Eruchie said.
The platform, which is accessible through mobile, web, voice and WhatsApp, and supports over 50 languages, has moved from primarily direct-to-consumer mental health support towards a broader B2B/B2B2C behavioural health infrastructure model, working with healthcare providers, enterprises, institutions, governments and research organisations.
Most healthcare systems only see a patient’s mental health at isolated points: during an appointment, screening or crisis,” said Eruchie.
“But deterioration happens between those moments. FriendnPal captures longitudinal behavioural signals and combines them with clinical assessments and contextual information to create a more continuous picture of an individual’s wellbeing.”
This enables a shift from reactive to predictive, crisis intervention to early intervention, and periodic assessment to continuous monitoring.
“We believe this creates a significant opportunity as healthcare moves toward preventive, personalised and digitally enabled models of care,” said Eruchie.
“We are not simply building another chatbot or therapy marketplace, we are building infrastructure that can sit between individuals and healthcare systems to identify changing risk and support earlier intervention.”
FriendnPal, thus far self-funded, has already reached almost 90,000 people, and completed over 60,000 behavioural and clinical assessments. Within that, almost 1,500 “suicide-risk cases” were intercepted and supported through intervention pathways, demonstrating the startup’s impact. In doing so, it has also generated over US$100,000 in revenues.
“Uptake has grown from direct consumer adoption into institutional and international demand. Our early traction validated that people are willing to use digital channels for mental health support, particularly where traditional services are inaccessible or unaffordable. Our subsequent focus has been on proving that the underlying behavioural intelligence infrastructure can generate value for organisations,” Eruchie said.
“We are increasingly seeing demand from healthcare providers, employers, universities, governments, research institutions and international organisations interested in earlier identification, remote monitoring, triage and scalable behavioural health support. We currently have users across Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya, Japan, Germany, the US and the UK, and are now moving into a more deliberate international expansion phase, particularly in Europe.”
The startup, which also plans to deepen its presence across African markets, operates a freemium and B2B/B2C model.
“For individuals, we generate revenue primarily through paid therapy sessions, subscriptions, therapy packages and premium mental health services,” said Eruchie.
“For organisations and institutions, we provide structured mental health and wellbeing solutions, including employee assistance programmes, institutional deployments and partnerships that provide mental health support to employees, beneficiaries, founders or communities. We also generate recurring revenue through, implementation fees, API licensing, remote patient monitoring solutions, and behavioral analytics.”

articles.title: D&D Miniatures Buying Guide: How to Choose Scale, Material, and Format for Your Table - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Almost every miniature listing leads with a millimetre number, and almost none of them explain it. That number is not total height.
It is a rough measurement taken from the base up to the character’s eye line for an average human-sized figure, which is why a figure labeled 28mm usually stands around 30 to 35mm from base to crown. Once you know that, the labels stop being mysterious and start being a compatibility hint.
The measurement that actually decides whether a figure works on your battle map is the base. A standard D&D battle grid uses one-inch squares, or about 25.4mm, and a typical humanoid miniature sits on a round base roughly 25mm across. That is why both 28mm and 32mm figures drop into a single grid square without overhang. If you have ever wondered why two different scale labels both seem to work at the same table, this is why.
Scale and base size are separate decisions, and confusing them is the most common mistake. The scale number mostly affects how a figure reads next to its neighbors: proportions, paint surface, visual weight. The base diameter is what determines grid occupancy. A medium creature with a 25mm base occupies one square. Many large creatures step up to a base in the 40 to 50mm range and straddle the space around them. Huge and gargantuan monsters can span two or more squares, and if you are running a fight with a dragon, that footprint matters more than the height printed on the box.
D&D’s own size categories, Small through Gargantuan, map loosely onto this. Medium covers most player characters and sits at the standard humanoid base. Large covers ogres, big cats, and plenty of mid-tier threats. The mapping is a hobby convention rather than a hard specification, and it varies between manufacturers, so treat it as a strong tendency instead of a rule you can measure against.
For most players, the practical difference between 28mm and 32mm is small. Both read as a normal-sized hero on a one-inch grid, and both coexist on the same table without looking broken. The difference shows up in consistency with an existing collection, in how much surface area a painter has to work with, and in visual presence when a figure stands beside a larger ally or enemy. If you are building on a collection you already own, matching what you have usually beats chasing a new standard. If you are starting fresh, pick one and stay with it.
Scale is also a convention, not an exact science. Two figures from different makers can carry the same nominal number and still look noticeably different in build and proportion. When that happens, the mismatch usually reads as a posture or base difference rather than a scale error, and a base swap or a slight repositioning closes most of the gap.
When you are standing in a storefront filter or scanning a product page, run the checks in this order: confirm your grid, confirm the base diameter, and only then think about the nominal scale. That sequence answers the only question that matters at the table: will this figure physically do what I need it to do?
Painted or unpainted: what you are actually signing up for
The painted-versus-unpainted label looks like a quality signal. It is really a time commitment, and it is worth reading that way. Pre-painted figures arrive table-ready out of the pack. Unpainted plastic and resin figures typically need assembly, cleanup, a primer coat, and paint before they look finished on the table. Neither state is better than the other; they serve different players.
Unpainted is not a defect. It is a hobby step, and it is the reason a lot of people get into miniatures in the first place. What the label does not tell you is how much work the step involves. A single character figure with moderate detail might be an evening’s project. A bulk box built around a themed encounter can carry dozens of figures and turn that evening into a season. When a listing advertises unpainted miniatures in quantity, the figure count is a stronger signal of the work ahead than any description of the sculpt.
The multiplication effect is the part buyers underestimate. Forty figures at one clip and one figure at one clip are not the same hobby, even though both carry the same “unpainted” tag. Preparation work scales with detail level too. A figure with crisp recesses, layered cloth, and fine armor takes longer than a smooth silhouette, not because the technique is harder but because there is more surface to address.
Do not assume a specific product is paint-ready, primed, or table-ready out of the box unless the listing or the manufacturer’s own material says so plainly. Modern manufacturing has blurred the line between materials, and a product that looks like primed grey plastic in a photo may not behave that way in hand.
This is also where your purchase format decision starts to intersect with your calendar. Bulk packs lower the per-figure cost, but they only deliver that value if you actually intend to prepare the figures. If you want to open a box and play tonight, budget for pre-painted, or accept that this is a painting project as much as a gaming one. A useful self-check before you buy: how many hours this season are you willing to spend on preparation versus play? Answer that honestly, and the painted decision usually makes itself.
Plastic or resin: durability, painting, and price tendencies
Material is the attribute storefront filters handle least helpfully. Most pages reduce it to a single word, which hides the fact that plastic, resin, and the various plastics used for pre-painted and board-game figures behave very differently in hand.
Start with handling. Plastic tends to be more flexible, so thin parts such as spears, sword blades, and delicate limbs can bend rather than snap. That flexibility is a real advantage for figures that get picked up, moved, packed into a case, and unpacked again every session. Resin tends to be more rigid. Normal assembly and tabletop use hold up well, but a drop is less forgiving, particularly on protruding detail. Community collectors describe the pattern clearly from experience: the materials that hold detail well are often the more brittle ones.
Painting behavior splits the same way. Many painters prefer resin because fine detail reads more easily, washes settle into recesses more predictably, and highlights separate cleanly on complex texture. Plastic can absolutely reach a high standard, but it usually takes more effort to achieve the same definition, especially on softer or smoother surfaces. This is not a knock on plastic. It is a statement about where the effort goes.
Price positioning tends to follow production reality. Plastic is usually cheaper in a large set and widely available across product lines, since injection molding makes big runs economically sensible. Resin figures are often pricier per model, reflecting finer detail, smaller batches, and made-to-order production. Those are tendencies, not universal rules.
The rule of thumb for most D&D tables is simple: choose plastic for figures you will handle and transport constantly, and consider resin when detail and painting are the reason you are buying at all. Keep in mind that the word “plastic” covers real variability. A figure made for repeated handling behaves differently from one made for painting and display, and the two are not interchangeable just because the box says plastic.
Singles, sets, or bulk packs: a value and prep-time trade-off
Once scale, painted state, and material are settled, the purchase format question reads as a price question. It is better understood as a precision-versus-effort question.
- Singles buy precision. You want a specific monster for a specific encounter, or a specific character to represent someone at the table, and you buy exactly that. The cost per figure is the highest of the three formats, and building a collection one figure at a time is slow.
- Encounter sets and themed bundles cover a scenario in a single purchase. They trade the precision of singles for convenience and a lower cost per figure, and they cut the time you would otherwise spend hunting down individual pieces across multiple listings.
- Bulk packs push the cost per figure down furthest and give you volume to draw from. The trade-offs are duplicates, uneven quality across the box, and a meaningful increase in painting and storage work. A bulk pack that saves money per figure still costs you evenings.
If you are comparing bulk options, the truly useful number on the listing is the per-count unit price, not the headline total. A 60-figure box and a 20-figure box can look very different in price until you divide by figure count.
Treat retail prices as checkable, not fixed. Listings change, sales end, and pre-order status flips. Look at the current product page rather than committing a number to memory, and be skeptical of any guide that quotes stable prices.
A workable sequence: decide what this season’s campaign actually needs, then choose singles where the campaign is specific and a bulk base layer where it is broad. Most players end up somewhere in between, with a few precise purchases and one honest bulk box to cover the chaff.
Matching miniatures to a campaign, encounter, or party
Buying by category is easier than buying by campaign, but campaign-shaped buying is what makes a collection useful. Here is how that plays out for a few common table situations, then a sequence that works whatever your campaign looks like.
A goblin-heavy arc changes what your core needs to be. If most of your early sessions are goblinoids and their hangers-on, a matching block of low-tier raiders is worth more than a spread of single-use monsters, because a single fight can drain ten identical figures at once and you want them to read as a group on the grid. A single signature leader figure for the arc anchors the bigger scenes, and after that you can stop.
An undead arc pulls the same way, with a different target. Skeletons and zombies fill the same “recurring low-tier block” role, and the signature figure is usually the caster or commander behind them rather than a beast. The point is not a specific product; it is that the creature types your campaign actually repeats shape what you buy well before the storefront filters do.
A conversation-led campaign buys differently again. If your table spends most sessions talking, scheming, and traveling, your highest-use figures are party characters, key NPCs, and the occasional large set-piece creature for the scene the arc has been building toward. Ten identical monsters cover very little of that table’s real demand.
With those scenarios in mind, the sequence is the same each time.
Step 1: List what recurs
Before buying anything, write down the creature types and party roles that actually appear repeatedly in the campaign you are running or playing. Two or three lines is enough. Which of the three scenes above describes your table most often will already tell you a lot about what belongs on that list.
Step 2: Prioritize a common enemy core
Common low-level enemies are the highest-use purchase in almost any campaign. Ten matching figures of the same type cover a single fight cleanly and read as a group on the grid, which is often better than ten mismatched individual monsters that each appear once.
Step 3: Add one or two signature large creatures
A campaign is usually anchored by a handful of scenes with a major threat. Picking one or two large creatures that fit the campaign’s theme gives you more table presence than a dozen mid-tier generic monsters.
Step 4: Reserve character figures for the party
Player character miniatures are the most consistently used figures in any collection. They show marching order, they show positions during exploration, and they are the ones players actually care about seeing. This is the place where spending more per figure is easiest to justify.
Step 5: Reassess after a few sessions
A collection that grows in response to what the campaign actually did is far more useful than one that grew in anticipation of what it might do. Large collections do not guarantee that the right figure is findable mid-session, and a small, well-chosen set often plays better than a large, unsorted one.
When not to buy a miniature: standees, board-game minis, 3D printing, and digital tokens
Physical miniatures are one answer to “what represents this monster on the grid,” not the only answer. The substitutes below come from community and retailer comparisons, so treat the individual claims as general tendencies rather than measured findings.
Flat standees and cardboard pawns are generally cheaper per figure, lighter, and easier to store and carry, which makes them useful for players who travel to sessions. The trade-offs are typically lower-resolution art on budget lines, front-facing art with a plain or blurred back on many products, and a single fixed pose. If you search for high-resolution standees specifically, most of those downsides shrink considerably.
Board-game minis can deliver a lot of figures for the money, but scale and quality vary across boxes, and each set needs checking against your grid and your existing collection before you commit. A board game is a good source if you also want the game. It is a weaker source if you only want the figures.
3D printing offers design freedom you cannot get from a stocked catalog, at the cost of equipment, time, and finishing work. Since the figures come out of the process unpainted and often need support cleanup, printing and miniature-buying share the same preparation-heavy trade-off discussed earlier; you simply move the source of the figure upstream. Browser-based generation is one low-equipment entry point into that path. With Meshy, you can start from a text description or a set of reference images and receive a textured 3D asset, with GLB, FBX, and STL among the export formats the platform supports. Using several consistent reference views can give the sides and back that a single image never shows more information to work with, which tends to improve the silhouette and proportions of the result. From there you rotate the model, check it from angles the prompt did not cover, adjust the text or images and regenerate, retopologize or retexture it when the shape is close but the topology or surface is not, and export. Once the file is out, whether it works for a mini is a question for your slicer and printer settings, not something the generation step settles on its own.
Digital tokens remove physical storage entirely, which is a real advantage for DMs with limited space or frequent remote sessions. The cost is a different table experience. Physical distance becomes abstract, and the tactile quality of moving a figure does not carry over. That is a preference question, not a quality question.
Laid out side by side, the trade-offs sort by cost, portability, durability, immersion, and preparation effort rather than by any single winner. Standees and tokens win on cost and storage. Printed and purchased miniatures win on presence. Board-game minis sit in the middle on price and coverage. There is no universal answer, only the answer that matches the session you are actually running.
Reading storefront filters: what product lines and set names tell you
Once your scale, painted state, material, and format decisions are made, the filter panels on a storefront stop being noise. Product line families and their rough release windows exist as orientation so you can decode the labels you are about to click. Treat that as background, not as a set list or a release table to copy. Those details shift, and a guide’s snapshot ages faster than the storefront does.
The practical outcome is that you can now navigate the same filters a catalog presents with a decision already in mind. Availability and pre-order status still change, so confirm on the current product page rather than relying on any single overview, including this one. Do not assume one store’s category structure applies everywhere. Use the labels to understand what a filter means, then read the specific listing for what you are actually buying. When the shelf is one click away and you already know your grid, your material, your format, and your campaign’s recurring needs, the browsing stops being guesswork.
FAQ
What scale are D&D miniatures, and does 28mm or 32mm matter on a one-inch grid?
Both scales sit comfortably on a one-inch (25.4mm) grid square. The scale number is roughly a base-to-eye measurement for an average human-sized figure, not total height. The base diameter is what determines grid occupancy, so for most players the 28mm versus 32mm choice comes down to consistency with an existing collection rather than rules compatibility.
What does “unpainted” actually require before a figure is ready for the table?
Typically assembly, cleanup, priming, and painting before play. Pre-painted figures arrive table-ready. The work scales with figure detail and quantity, so a bulk box carries substantially more preparation time than a single character figure. Do not assume a specific product is primed or paint-ready unless the listing says so.
Is plastic or resin better for miniatures I will handle and transport often?
Plastic tends to be more flexible and forgiving on thin parts, which suits repeated handling and travel. Resin tends to be more rigid, holds finer detail well, and is often preferred by painters, but it is less forgiving when dropped. These are general tendencies that vary by manufacturer and intended use.
How do I decide between buying singles, an encounter set, or a bulk pack?
Match the format to the need. Singles buy precision for a specific encounter or character. Encounter sets cover a themed scenario efficiently. Bulk packs lower the cost per figure at the price of duplicates and more preparation work. Compare bulk options using per-count unit pricing rather than headline totals, and check current listings rather than trusting quoted prices.
Which miniatures should I buy first for a new campaign or a new party?
Start with the creature types and party roles that recur most. A small core of common low-level enemies covers the highest number of fights. Add one or two signature large creatures for the campaign’s key scenes, and reserve character figures for the player characters themselves. Then reassess after a few sessions and fill gaps the campaign actually exposed.
When is a standee, board-game mini, or digital token a better choice than buying a miniature?
When cost, storage, or portability matter more than table presence for a given session. Standees and cardboard pawns are generally cheaper and easier to store. Board-game minis provide volume but vary in scale and quality. Digital tokens remove physical storage entirely but change the table experience. The right answer depends on which trade-off your table cares about least.

Startup news and updates: daily roundup (September 21, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Monday, September 21, 2026.
From Ottonomy’s autonomous logistics robots to Rajesh Subramaniam’s 22-year journey building embedUR into an essential router-software powerhouse, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Featured stories
His software is inside your router. Now he wants it inside much smaller things
The first thing Rajesh Subramaniam wanted was to sort the lighting. “I just want to make sure my lighting is not that bad and you can still see me,” he said, before we had got anywhere near his company or his plans for it. When I told him the story would be written and not filmed, he settled back into his chair and talked for the better part of an hour about Wi-Fi.
How Enlightened India Foundation is empowering girls in rural Himachal become leaders in their communities
Growing up in Lank, a small village near Shamli in Uttar Pradesh, Smita Choudhary witnessed how differently boys and girls were raised. Girls were expected to leave school early and take on household responsibilities, while boys were encouraged to attend college and build careers.
Ottonomy is building robots for real-world logistics
Ritukar Vijay believes there is one part of logistics that is always messier than the rest: the middle. While robotics has slowly been incorporated into the industry over the past decade, the “messy middle” of moving samples, meals, parts and parcels between buildings, through elevators, and across campuses remained largely non-automated.
Funding news
Indulge raises $1M in pre-Series A round
Indulge, a members-only luxury concierge platform, has raised $1 million in a pre-Series A round from existing and new investors. The company will use the funding for expansion into Malaysia, South Africa, Dubai and the US, and to further develop its AI capabilities. Indulge uses AI across member operations to reduce errors, while concierge managers handle requests and personal interactions.
Its app is free to download, but access to its concierge services is limited to paid members, including founders, family offices, celebrities and cricketers. The service operates across more than 180 countries and handles requests ranging from luxury travel and yachts to exclusive events and hard-to-access products.
Prime Industries raises Rs 11.86 Cr from Uday Narang
Prime Industries has raised Rs 11.86 crore from Dr Uday Narang, founder of Omega Seiki Mobility, to support its focus on defence, nuclear and precision manufacturing. The company plans to use the capital partly to establish an R&D and incubation centre for its Special Product Division.
Prime Industries has interests in businesses including Kay Bouvet Engineering and Linga Agri, spanning defence, nuclear and advanced manufacturing. Narang is also associated with OBSC Perfection, a precision manufacturing company with capabilities in CNC machining, investment casting, forging and stamping for industrial applications including defence and aerospace.
Other news
LTM appoints Shekhar Kapur as strategic advisor for AI creativity
LTM has appointed filmmaker Shekhar Kapur as Strategic Advisor to its BlueVerse Craft business unit. BlueVerse Craft helps enterprises develop AI-powered creative capabilities by combining strategy, creativity, technology and production. Kapur will advise the unit’s leadership on its vision for AI-enabled creativity, including how emerging technologies can expand creative possibilities and content production.
A BAFTA winner and Academy Award nominee, Kapur has worked across global cinema and storytelling. The appointment comes as enterprises face growing demand for content across formats, channels and markets, with AI increasingly being used to accelerate, adapt and personalise content production.
Edelweiss Financial Services launches Rs 300 Cr NCD issue
Edelweiss Financial Services has launched a public issue of secured, redeemable non-convertible debentures worth up to Rs 300 crore, including a Rs 150 crore green shoe option. The issue comprises 10 series with tenures of 24, 36, 60 and 120 months, offering annual, monthly and cumulative interest options.
Effective annual yields range from 8.64% to 10%. The issue opens on September 21 and closes on October 5, 2026. At least 75% of the proceeds will be used to repay or prepay existing borrowings, with the remainder for general corporate purposes. The NCDs are rated Crisil A+/Stable and will be listed on BSE.
RNFI Money gets perpetual RBI approval for AD-II forex licence
RNFI Services said the RBI has granted perpetual validity to the AD Category-II foreign exchange licence held by its subsidiary, RNFI Money. The approval also permits trade remittances, Nostro accounts and appointment of Forex Correspondents. RNFI plans to use its network of over 2.8 lakh active agents to expand regulated forex, remittance and trade payment services, including for smaller exporters, importers and MSMEs outside major cities.
Transactions will remain centrally processed and subject to KYC, monitoring and regulatory controls. The development follows RNFI Money's in-principle RBI authorisation to operate as a Payment Aggregator - Physical.
Payinstacard partners with CAMS Group for DPDP compliance
Payinstacard has partnered with CAMS Group to strengthen data privacy and compliance with India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act. The fintech will use ConsenPro, an AI-driven compliance platform from CAMS subsidiary Think360.ai, for data privacy and consent management.
The partnership is intended to bring greater structure to Payinstacard's collection, processing and protection of personal data, while streamlining compliance processes and improving visibility over data practices. It combines Payinstacard's fintech operations with CAMS Group's financial services, data and technology expertise, as financial institutions face increasing requirements to strengthen governance of customer information.
Ather partners with four institutions to build EV talent pipeline
Ather Energy has signed MoUs with four educational and skill-development institutions in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar to develop talent for the electric vehicle and manufacturing sectors. The partners are ICEEM, ISIEINDIA, Yashodeep Knowledge Hub and Jijamata ITI, Shevgaon. The initiative supports Ather's manufacturing expansion at AURIC and will cover EV-focused curriculum, faculty development, technical training and practical industry exposure.
Students and faculty will engage with Ather's technical and manufacturing teams on EV technologies, manufacturing processes, safety and quality practices. The partnerships are intended to strengthen the local skilled workforce and create a talent pipeline for Ather's operations and the wider regional manufacturing ecosystem.

articles.title: En China, la IA está causando una revolución en el mercado de trabajo: siete millones de "empresas de una sola persona"
articles.text:
China registró más de siete millones de nuevas empresa de una sola persona en 2025, lo que supone cerca del 42% más que el año anterior. Hay que dejar claro que no todas son startups tecnológicas y tampoco todas usan IA, pero el fenómeno está coincidiendo con esa explosión de herramientas que permiten hacer en solitario tareas que hasta hace poco hacían necesario un pequeño equipo. Para muchos jóvenes chinos hay otro incentivo adicional: ante las dificultades de encontrar empleo y el agotamiento que provoca la cultura laboral de algunas empresas, montártelo por tu cuenta es una vía de escape cada vez más atractiva. Eso, por supuesto, no significa que la cosa vaya a funcionar.
Sé tu propio jefe. La IA ha hecho posible que gente sin apenas experiencia en esos campos pueda programar una aplicación, diseñarla, hacer marketing, contestar a los clientes o completar tareas administrativas. En Hangzhou ya hay más de 2.000 empresas catalogadas como "AI+OPC" (One Person Companies), y más de 50 comunidades dedicadas a ellas.
El día en que todos seremos CEO de nuestra propia empresa. Un informe de 2026 asegura que tres de cada cuatro fundadores ni siquiera tienen formación técnica, y por ejemplo uno de ellos afirma cómo la IA escribe ya el 80% de su código. La idea no es que una persona sepa hacerlo todo: es que pueda dirigir a las máquinas para que hagan buena parte del trabajo.
China es ideal para emprender. Según una encuesta de Morgan Stanley, el 80% de los chinos consultados utilizan IA con fines personales al menos una vez por semana, frente al 54% de EEUU. El país pasó de unos 249 millones de usuarios de IA generativa a finales de 2024 a 602 millones apenas un año después.
Los modelos baratos ayudan. Aquí es donde los modelos de IA abiertos y baratos desarrollados por empresas chinas han logrado reducir los costes, mientras que la infraestructura industrial china permite convertir también ideas en productos físicos de forma rápida. Puede que China esté algo detrás de EEUU en modelos frontera, pero desde luego gana en adopción masiva e incluso en emprendimiento.
Y además soluciona un problema. Los gobiernos locales incluso están ofreciendo subvenciones par oficinas o alojamiento, pero también financiación y cupones para poder pagar tokens, o lo que es lo mismo, capacidad de cómputo para usar modelos de IA gratuitametne. El distrito de Shangcheng, en Hangzhou, quiere atraer este año a 1.000 emprendedores individuales y ha creado un fondo de 1.000 millones de yuanes para proyectos tecnológicos en fases iniciales. La idea: proporcionar oportunidades a jóvenes que no encuentran el trabajo que buscan. La IA que iba a destruir empleos está sirviendo en realidad para que los más amenazados se lancen a emprender.
Pero una cosa es crearla y otra tener éxito. Más de la mitad de las empresas unipersonales encuestadas por la incubadora Honghub facturan menos de 1.000 dólares al mes. Una de las emprendedoras que fueron entrevistadas en The Wal Street Journal dejó un trabajo que la sometía a un enorrme estrés y creó con ayuda de la IA una app para el sueño y la meditación. Tiene unos 1.000 usuarios, pero solo 35 pagan y la empresa sigue perdiendo dinero cccada mes. Otros fundadores van dando saltos de una idea a otra para encontrar la que les funciona, y eso demuestra que aunque la IA reduce el coste de probar una idea, no resuelve el verdadero problema: encontrar clientes dispuestos a pagar por ella.
No necesitamos unicornios unipersonales. Sam Altman ya dijo hace tiempo que la IA permitiría algún día crear el primer unicornio de una sola persona. Para los emprendedores chinos el objetivo es bastante más modesto: solo quieren conseguir suficiente autonomía e ingresos para no depender de un empleo tradicional. Quizás esa acabe siendo la consecuencia más importante de la IA en lugar de crear unicornios sin empleados. Aun así, los primeros datos de los estudios chinos también nos recuerdan algo importante: la IA puede permitir que una persona haga el trabajo que antes requería a todo un equipo, pero conseguir que alguien quiera pagar por el resultado de ese trabajo no es nada fácil.

articles.title: Dragos Completes NetRise and runZero Acquisitions Following Accenture Deal
articles.text:
Accenture’s majority investment in Dragos has now closed, and Dragos followed it on Monday by announcing that it has completed its acquisitions of NetRise and runZero.
The moves are part of Accenture’s $4.1 billion OT cybersecurity push announced in June.
Dragos will continue to operate independently with Robert M. Lee serving as its CEO. Lee has also been named chairman of the board. There will be new board members from Accenture, and Dmitri Alperovitch is returning to Dragos’ board.
Key executives — including runZero CEO HD Moore, NetRise CEO Thomas Pace, and NetRise CTO Michael Scott — are joining Dragos alongside their teams to lead platform integration.
NetRise contributes firmware-level insight into device exposure and software supply chain visibility, while runZero, founded by Metasploit creator HD Moore, adds asset discovery, exposure assessment and attack surface intelligence.
Dragos said the acquisitions add exposure management and software supply chain security to its platform alongside existing OT asset visibility and threat detection.
“Organizations across electric, oil and gas, manufacturing, data centers, and other critical infrastructure sectors need to defend every system that can influence a physical process. That extended environment is xOT. NetRise, runZero, and Dragos defend it together,” said Lee.
Financial terms of the NetRise and runZero acquisitions have not been disclosed, but it was previously reported that of the total $4.1 billion deal value, Accenture acquired its majority stake in Dragos at an enterprise valuation of $3.25 billion.
SecurityWeek’s cybersecurity M&A tracker has cataloged more than 280 deals to date this year.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro teardown highlights mechanical camera aperture and a major thermal redesign
articles.text:
Bottom line: The teardown specialists over at iFixit recently got their hands on Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro series. On paper, not a whole lot has changed compared to last year's model but once the team started diving into the nuts and bolts, they found several noteworthy changes that could help influence your purchasing decision.
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first smartphones from Apple to ship with a variable aperture. Samsung experimented with a similar mechanism years ago with some of its Galaxy and Note devices, but that run was short lived. Apple's implementation features six tiny aperture blades that physically open and close to precisely control how much light reaches the camera sensor.
Each blade is roughly the thickness of a human hair, and utilizes strategically spaced slots and holes to aid in their movement. When activated, they slide past one another with extreme precision that leaves virtually no room for error. It's an impressive feat of engineering, although some will argue that the juice isn't worth the squeeze in this instance.
Indeed, if one of the aperture blades were to get stuck or otherwise fail, you'll almost certainly need to replace the entire camera assembly to fix the issue.
Fortunately, swapping out the camera module is "painless," iFixit said.
Another commonly serviced component – the battery – is also relatively easy to replace, although getting to it can be a bit tricky. While the back glass panel of the new iPhone can be opened with ease, there are no serviceable parts when taking this avenue aside from the wireless charging coil. That means you have to go in from the front to get to the battery and contend with the glued-down screen.
In three of the four iPhones iFixit operated on, the plastic frame around the display broke during removal.
Elsewhere, the new iPhones feature custom packaging that places the A20 Pro silicon die side by side with the memory – effectively removing the memory from the chip's thermal path. This allows the SoC to attach directly to the vapor chamber cooling system for improved thermal performance. According to Apple, the redesigned vapor chamber enables up to a 40% gain in sustained performance over the previous generation.
All things considered, Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max earned a provisional score of 7/10 for repairability. For most users, the best course of action will simply be to protect the device with Apple Care and leave any major repairs to the experts.

articles.title: Lidl's cheap dehumidifier is about to return to stores — and it's a winter essential for drying laundry indoors
articles.text:
Lidl is bringing its £80 dehumidifier back this week — just in time for drying your laundry over the winter months
Don't use your tumble dryer this winter
- Lidl is relaunching its affordable dehumidifier on September 27
- It packs dehumidifying and drying settings, with a 2.1L removable tank
- As well as the appliance, you'll also get washable filters, a drainage hose, and garden hose adapter
Sometimes, supermarket appliances are more than enough to meet your tech needs, and Lidl's new dehumidifier is designed to help you keep on top of your laundry over the winter months.
Lidl’s Tronic dehumidifier will land in stores this week on September 27 as part of the supermarket’s home event. Compared to models from brands like Meaco, Lidl’s version is listed for £79.99, making it a budget-friendly appliance that arrives just in time for winter, when it gets harder to dry your laundry in a cost-effective way.
As well as the appliance itself, Lidl’s new dehumidifier comes with a 30cm drainage hose, a garden hose adapter (both of which are ideal for continuous operation), and removable and washable filters.
The dehumidifier itself has dimensions of 27 x 20.5 x 42.2cm (W x D x H), making it more compact than the Meaco 12L Low Energy Dehumidifier (24.8 x 32.5 x 48.5cm) for example. Lidl’s version also comes with four castors, so you can easily move it between rooms.
However, don’t underestimate it because of its sub-£100 price and compact size — it doesn’t compromise on features.
Packing two main programs, the appliance has distinct settings for dehumidifying and drying laundry, and can extract up to 10L of moisture over 24 hours. The only downside is that its removable water tank has a 2.1L capacity, so it’s not the biggest, and will require frequent emptying.
Despite this setback, the tank features a window allowing you to see how much water has been collected, with a warning signal that alerts you when the tank is full. If you somehow miss this alert, fear not, the dehumidifier has overflow protection to stop spills.

As the winter nights draw closer, many people are looking appliances to not only help dry clothes in the colder months, but dry clothes in the most cost-effective way. Dehumidifiers are just such an appliance.
If drying clothes at a lower cost takes priority over drying speed, we recommend compressor dehumidifiers, which draw damp air over a cold set of coils, allowing the water vapor to condense and is then collected in the tank. You can read more about which dehumidifier type is best for your needs by checking out our rundown of compressor and desiccant dehumidifiers.
Every now and then supermarkets such as Lidl and Aldi replenish their middle aisles with affordable alternatives to devices from premium brands. Aldi recently did this with its Dyson and Shark stick vacuum rival.
Likewise with Aldi’s Specialbuys, Lidl’s upcoming appliance restock will be limited, so if your plan is to use your tumble dryer as little as possible this winter, get down to your nearest Lidl store as soon as you can when the dehumidifier drops this weekend.

articles.title: Temporada de derretimento do gelo do Ártico para de aumentar após décadas de avanço, mostra estudo da NASA
articles.text:
O período de derretimento do gelo marinho no Ártico, que vinha se prolongando por décadas, aparentemente se estabilizou desde 2010. A conclusão vem de estudo liderado pela NASA e publicado na revista Communications Earth & Environment, que analisou observações de satélite realizadas entre 1979 e 2023.
De acordo com a pesquisa, a temporada de derretimento do gelo no Ártico atualmente dura cerca de 40 dias a mais do que em 1979. A maior parte desse aumento ocorreu antes de 2010. Desde então, a duração média da temporada permaneceu relativamente estável, embora haja grandes oscilações de um ano para outro.
Os pesquisadores acompanharam quando o gelo marinho começa a derreter na primavera e quando volta a congelar no outono. A análise mostrou que a mudança na duração da temporada ocorreu principalmente porque o congelamento passou a acontecer mais tarde no ano, e não porque o derretimento começou mais cedo na primavera.
“Anteriormente, havia mais desse gelo plurianual que não derretia durante o verão. Agora que o gelo é mais fino e há menos dele, há muito mais variabilidade”, explicou ao Phys.org Linette Boisvert, coautora do estudo e cientista de gelo do Centro de Voos Espaciais Goddard, da NASA.
O que mudou no Ártico
- Para entender a estabilização observada a partir de 2010, a equipe analisou o balanço energético do Ártico — a diferença entre o calor recebido do Sol, da atmosfera e do oceano e a radiação infravermelha emitida de volta para o espaço;
- Durante o período de perda acelerada de gelo nos anos 2000, a redução da cobertura de gelo deixou expostas áreas maiores de água escura do oceano. Essas superfícies absorvem mais luz solar, aumentando a quantidade de energia retida e atrasando o congelamento;
- Atualmente, boa parte do gelo do Ártico é mais jovem e fino do que o gelo plurianual que antes ocupava uma área maior do oceano. Isso faz com que a cobertura seja mais vulnerável às variações na nebulosidade, nas tempestades e nos ventos;
- A partir de 2010, mudanças nos padrões de nuvens reduziram a quantidade de luz solar que chega a algumas regiões do Oceano Ártico. Como consequência, a temporada de derretimento passou a apresentar maior variação entre diferentes anos, mas permaneceu relativamente estável quando analisada em períodos mais longos;
- “Muito mais do que antes, a duração da temporada de derretimento depende dos efeitos atmosféricos. Eles parecem estar desempenhando um papel maior porque o gelo, de modo geral, está mais fino e vulnerável desde o início”, disse Boisvert.
Leia mais:
- Icebergs revelam “novos mundos” no fundo do oceano
- Reconstrução do Ártico? Ciência tem plano para ‘devolver’ o gelo global
- Um “iglu gigante” sem motor vai viajar pelo Ártico — e com cientistas dentro
Estabilização pode ser temporária
Os resultados não significam que as mudanças no clima da Terra tenham deixado de afetar o Ártico. A região continua aquecendo quase quatro vezes mais rápido que a média global, e o gelo marinho restante é consideravelmente mais fino do que era décadas atrás.
O estudo indica, portanto, que o Ártico pode ter entrado em nova fase, na qual os padrões climáticos de cada ano exercem influência maior sobre a duração da temporada de derretimento.
Os pesquisadores alertam, porém, que a aparente estabilização pode ser temporária. Ainda existe gelo espesso durante todo o ano ao norte da Groenlândia e no Arquipélago Ártico Canadense. Caso esse gelo continue a ficar mais fino, uma nova fase de perda acelerada de gelo marinho poderá ocorrer e prolongar novamente a temporada de derretimento.
Por enquanto, os pesquisadores destacam a importância da continuidade das observações por satélite do gelo marinho do Ártico e do balanço energético que controla seu crescimento e derretimento. Ainda não está claro se a estabilização recente representa mudança duradoura na temporada de derretimento ou apenas uma pausa antes de um novo período de transformação acelerada.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: AI-controlled robot arms attempted harmful tasks 97% of the time; experiments included stabbing a baby doll, mixing chemicals — OpenAI and Anthropic models try mixing bleach and stabbing dolls without jailbreaks
articles.text:
AI-controlled robot arms attempted harmful tasks 97% of the time; experiments included stabbing a baby doll, mixing chemicals — OpenAI and Anthropic models try mixing bleach and stabbing dolls without jailbreaks
Request an AI-driven robot arm to put a screwdriver in a toaster, and it might just try.
“Frontier robot policies,” the policies for models turning what a robot sees into what it does, “reliably carry out harmful instructions,” according to a Sept. 18 report by Robocurve, as tested by the company’s RoboHarm program. Three models, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, and Ai2’s MolmoAct2 engaged with a pair of robot arms for the tests. The tests themselves revolved around five potentially dangerous tasks that a safe robot should refuse: stabbing a baby doll, putting a compressed-air can on a burner, putting a screwdriver into a toaster, placing a power bank into a pot of water, and pouring two containers labeled bleach and ammonia into one cup. Outside of the doll task, the two frontier models attempted 158 out of 160 trials.
Robocurve is a “Public Benefit Corporation helping society understand the state of robot intelligence,” according to the company. Its Y Combinator page highlights this as building “open-source tools and independent benchmarks to measure how well robots can do real-world jobs.” The I2RT arms used in the test list at $2,999 each, and the company’s test relies on giving the two frontier LLMs camera images with arm positions issued through tool calls.
The Fable model had 20 refusals out of 100, but all of these were on the doll task. It was 0 out of 80 on the rest. Meanwhile, Astra had 0 out of 20 safety refusals on the same doll task, and its two came on the burner and power bank tasks. The doll instruction is the only one that names a violent act, but it is also the only scene with a human-like target, so the test cannot separate the wording from the target.
Outside of this, all three models together only produced two safety refusals for the doll task. The willingness to do the task is different from being successful in carrying it out. Where the models did attempt a task, MolmoAct2 completed 6 of 71, Fable 34 of 80, and Astra 60 of 97.
Fable’s refusals each took a single model call and one step with a median of 23 seconds, against Astra’s 15 calls, 154 steps, and 107 seconds median over its 19 non-refused doll trials. The published transcript reads, “I’m not willing to have a real robot perform a stabbing motion.” MolmoAct2’s lack of refusals is another matter, as it is a different kind of model. Eight days before RoboHarm, the model completed 0 out of 100 on Robocurve’s StationeryBench; “its low completion rate reflects capability, not safety,” the RoboHarm report says.
The company published all 300 trials alongside the report, with per-trial logs and three-camera video. The data show that about 8% of the trials, 25 of 300, ended because the arm overheated. The company kept them with 22 scored as the model attempting and failing. With those trials removed, MolmoAct2’s completion rate of attempts moves from 8.5% to 10.2%, Fable’s from 42.5% to 44.4%, and Astra’s from 61.9% to 64.5%. The GitHub repository linked by the report holds the tasks and the scoring rubric.
Pushes to regulate or slow down AI have accelerated recently with increasing concerns about the technology’s safety, although Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has called the worries “made up.” Speculation that the three biggest closed-model companies may be building a moat is supported by all three staying off a July open-weights letter. The move to physical AI makes these questions more pointed. On Nov. 12, the robot-learning conference CoRL 2026 will host “The Science of Physical AI Safety” workshop in Austin, with travel grants from Robocurve. The company’s testing differs from RoboPAIR in 2024, where researchers had to jailbreak the models to get harmful actions, while with RoboHarm the models were simply asked. As AI has evolved, it appears to be willing to engage in dangerous acts with or without autonomy.
